  vals <- as.numeric(unlist(regmatches(x, gregexpr("[0-9]+\\.?[0-9]*", x))))
  sprintf("%.1f%% (95%% CI %.1f%% to %.1f%%)", vals[1], vals[2], vals[3])

  x_num <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  if (!is.finite(x_num)) {
    x
  } else if (x_num < 0.001) {
    "<0.001"
  } else {
    sprintf("%.3f", x_num)
  }
}

}

build_publication_flextable <- function(data,
                                        footer_lines = c("Source: Kenya DHS 2022. Survey-weighted estimates."),
                                        font_size = 9,
                                        header_labels = NULL,
                                        spanner_values = NULL,
                                        spanner_widths = NULL) {

  if (!is.null(header_labels)) {
    ft <- flextable::set_header_labels(ft, values = header_labels)
  }

  if (!is.null(spanner_values) && !is.null(spanner_widths)) {
    ft <- flextable::add_header_row(
      ft,
      values = spanner_values,
      colwidths = spanner_widths,
      top = TRUE
    )
  }

  ft <- ft %>%
    flextable::set_table_properties(layout = "autofit", opts_word = list(split = TRUE)) %>%
    flextable::autofit() %>%
    flextable::fit_to_width(max_width = 7.1) %>%
    flextable::theme_booktabs() %>%
    flextable::font(fontname = "Times New Roman", part = "all") %>%
    flextable::fontsize(size = font_size, part = "all") %>%
    flextable::bold(part = "header") %>%
    flextable::align(align = "left", part = "all") %>%
    flextable::align(j = seq_len(ncol(data)), align = "center", part = "header") %>%
    flextable::align(j = 1, align = "left", part = "header") %>%
    flextable::valign(valign = "top", part = "all") %>%
    flextable::padding(padding = 3, part = "all")

  if (length(footer_lines) > 0) {
    ft <- flextable::add_footer_lines(ft, values = footer_lines) %>%
      flextable::merge_h(part = "footer") %>%
      flextable::italic(part = "footer") %>%
      flextable::fontsize(size = 8, part = "footer") %>%
      flextable::align(align = "left", part = "footer")
  }

  ft
}

Nichodemus Werre Amollo^1,\*^, Japheth Ogol^1,2^

^1^ School of Health Sciences, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga University of Science and Technology, Bondo, Kenya\
^2^ Department of Family Medicine & Population Health (FAMPOP), University of Antwerp, Wilrijk, Belgium

*Correspondence: Nichodemus Werre Amollo, nwere@ejooust.ac.ke

# Abstract

**Background:** Kenya replaced the National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) with the Social Health Authority (SHA) on 1 October 2024. KDHS 2022 therefore provides the last nationally representative population baseline before the transition. Earlier Kenyan DHS analyses mainly focused on women of reproductive age rather than the full household population across life stages.

**Methods:** We conducted a cross-sectional secondary analysis of the KDHS 2022 person recode file. The analytic sample included de-facto household members with valid insurance responses from the full household questionnaire subsample. We estimated survey-weighted prevalence of coverage, service use, and payment at the last outpatient visit, and quantified out-of-pocket (OOP) depth from cleaned continuous cost variables. Wealth-related inequality was summarised with concentration indices, Erreygers-corrected estimates, the slope and relative indices of inequality (SII, RII), and decomposed by the Wagstaff method. Survey-weighted quasi-Poisson models estimated adjusted prevalence ratios (APR). We assessed linkage with household social assistance and compared coverage with KDHS 2014. We additionally fitted an intersectional multilevel (MAIHDA) model and a survey-cluster mixed-effects model, and microsimulated SHA premium-subsidy scenarios on the concentration index. Geolocating all 1,691 clusters, we modelled exclusion as a smooth function of location using binomial additive models and mapped the probability that it exceeds 90%.

**Results:** The analytic sample comprised `r format(analysis_object$overall_n, big.mark = ",")` de-facto household members. Any insurance coverage was `r fmt_pct_string(get_t1("All household members", "Any insurance % (95% CI)"))`, leaving `r fmt_pct_string(get_t1("All household members", "Uninsured % (95% CI)"))` uninsured. Coverage was lowest among young adults aged 18-24 at `r fmt_pct_string(get_t2("18-24", "All: insured % (95% CI)"))`, compared with `r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Children under 18"))` among children under 18 and `r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Older adults 60+"))` among adults aged 60 years and above. The wealth gradient was steep, from `r fmt_pct_string(get_t3("Wealth quintile", "Poorest"))` in the poorest quintile to `r fmt_pct_string(get_t3("Wealth quintile", "Richest"))` in the richest (ratio `r wealth_ratio`x). Richest-versus-poorest APR was `r get_t5("Model A: All ages", "Wealth: Richest")` in the all-ages model. The overall standard concentration index was `r fmt_ci_inline("All household members", "standard")`, the SII was `r get_t7("All household members", "SII, pp (95% CI)")` percentage points, and the RII was `r get_t7("All household members", "RII (95% CI)")`; decomposition attributed the inequality overwhelmingly to the wealth quintile itself. Among recent outpatient users, cash met `r cost_val("opd_overall_cost", "Cash share of cost, %")`% of total outpatient cost and NHIF only `r cost_val("opd_overall_cost", "NHIF share of cost, %")`%, with little difference between insured and uninsured users. `r top_uninsured_sentence` the most over-represented group among uninsured persons. Intersectional analysis attributed `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * analysis_object$maihda_vpc_null)`% of coverage variation to differences between strata, almost all additive, and a subsidy microsimulation showed that enrolling the two poorest quintiles reversed the concentration index from pro-rich (`r sprintf("%.4f", analysis_object$sim_baseline_ci)`) to pro-poor, leaving an uninsured "missing middle". Location stayed predictive after adjusting for settlement type and wealth; 55.6% of sampled land area had at least 80% probability of exceeding 90% exclusion, and county estimates ranged from 94.7% uninsured in Tana River to 54.0% in Nairobi.

**Conclusions:** Before SHA, Kenya had low coverage, extreme wealth-related inequality, and high payment exposure at outpatient contact. Young adults, children, the poorest households, and people with severe functional difficulty remained vulnerable in different ways. SHA monitoring should track life-course coverage, disability-sensitive access, geography, and payment exposure, not enrolment alone.

**Keywords:** Kenya DHS; health insurance; Social Health Authority; NHIF; wealth inequality; concentration index; disability; young adults; outpatient payment; universal health coverage

# Background

Kenya's transition from the National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) to the Social Health Authority (SHA) on 1 October 2024 is the country's most consequential health financing reform in recent years [@socialhealthinsuranceact2023; @shigeneralregulations2024]. NHIF was established as a statutory health insurer and became the main national vehicle for health insurance expansion, but its membership and effective benefit reach remained shaped by formal-sector employment, contributory payment capacity, provider contracting, and reimbursement arrangements [@barasa2018; @mbau2020]. Kenya expanded NHIF benefits and purchasing reforms over time, including capitation and contracting mechanisms intended to move the system toward universal health coverage (UHC), yet analyses of these reforms documented persistent gaps between enrolment, service availability, provider payment, and financial protection [@barasa2018; @mbau2020; @barasa2018sdg]. These implementation limits are not unique to Kenya. International experience shows that health insurance expansion in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) can increase nominal coverage while leaving substantial inequalities where entitlement depends on contributions, administrative registration, or facility-level purchasing arrangements [@lagomarsino2012; @kutzin2013; @hooley2022].

SHA was introduced to replace NHIF with a broader financing architecture that includes the Social Health Insurance Fund, the Primary Healthcare Fund, and the Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund [@socialhealthinsuranceact2023; @shigeneralregulations2024]. The reform created mandatory registration and pathways for government-financed coverage of indigent and vulnerable persons. For that reason, the immediate evaluation question is not only whether national enrolment rises after SHA, but whether groups previously outside the insurance system are actually reached. The 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS 2022) was conducted before SHA implementation and therefore provides the last nationally representative population baseline before the transition. A credible pre-SHA baseline is especially important because early reform monitoring can otherwise confuse progress from new registration drives with pre-existing inequalities inherited from NHIF.

Prior Kenyan DHS-based analyses provide important evidence, but their analytic populations and historical timing leave a gap for SHA monitoring. Kimani and colleagues used the 2008-09 KDHS to examine health insurance ownership among women and found strong gradients by wealth, education, age, marital status, and employment [@kimani2014]. Kazungu and Barasa used the 2008-09 and 2014 KDHS to examine levels, distribution, and correlates of health insurance coverage in Kenya, showing rising coverage but persistent socioeconomic inequality [@kazungu2017]. These studies established the core pattern that insurance coverage in Kenya was low and pro-rich. However, they relied mainly on standard adult recode files and earlier survey rounds, and therefore could not provide a full-population pre-SHA picture across children, men, older adults, household dependants, and people with functional difficulty. KDHS 2022 differs because insurance information is available in the Person Recode (PR) household-member file, enabling an all-population analysis of de-facto household members rather than only women of reproductive age or interviewed adults.

Regional evidence reinforces the need for sharper equity baselines. A multi-country analysis of 36 sub-Saharan African countries found that health insurance coverage remained low in most settings and was generally concentrated among wealthier, urban, and more educated groups [@barasa2021]. Such findings are consistent with broader UHC monitoring evidence showing that gains in service coverage and financial protection do not automatically move together [@who2023uhc; @wagstaff2018]. In Kenya, catastrophic health expenditure and impoverishing health payments have also been documented, underscoring that formal insurance coverage is only one component of financial protection [@chuma2012; @barasa2017catastrophic; @njagi2021]. KDHS 2022 cannot measure catastrophic spending directly, but it can identify whether routine outpatient contact still involved payment among insured and uninsured users. That is a useful early-warning indicator for benefit-design and purchasing problems under SHA.

The life-course dimension is also underdeveloped in the Kenyan insurance literature. Children may depend on household registration and parental or guardian enrolment, while young adults may move between parental dependency, schooling, informal work, and unstable employment. Evidence from LMICs shows that young people face barriers related to affordability, confidentiality, service acceptability, and fragmented transition into adult health systems [@nachiappan2022]. Older adults may have higher care needs but variable income, social support, and administrative capacity to maintain coverage. A single adult-only estimate can therefore hide different forms of exclusion across life stages. For SHA, these distinctions matter because registration pathways, dependant coverage, and public financing for vulnerable groups must operate across households rather than only through formal employment.

Disability adds another equity dimension. People with disabilities often have higher healthcare needs, greater transport and opportunity costs, and more frequent contact with health services, yet they may face administrative and financial barriers to insurance inclusion [@azizatunnisa2024]. A recent systematic review of LMIC evidence found that health insurance access among people with disabilities remains uneven and that insurance does not consistently translate into improved healthcare use, better health status, or financial protection [@azizatunnisa2024]. The Washington Group functioning approach allows disability-related access questions to be studied in household surveys, but Kenya-specific evidence linking functional difficulty, insurance coverage, outpatient use, and payment remains limited [@washington2016].

This study therefore aimed to characterize pre-SHA insurance coverage, wealth-related inequality, and payment at outpatient contact across the Kenyan population using KDHS 2022. Specifically, we examined four questions: first, what was the population-wide level of insurance coverage before SHA; second, how did coverage vary across life stages and policy-priority groups; third, which covariates remained associated with insurance coverage after adjustment; and fourth, how unequal was insurance coverage across the wealth distribution using concentration indices, Erreygers-corrected estimates, and absolute and relative inequality metrics. The contribution is not another generic determinants analysis; it is an all-population, policy-ready baseline of who was left outside Kenya's insurance system immediately before the SHA transition.

# Methods

## Study design and reporting

We conducted a cross-sectional secondary analysis of KDHS 2022 and report the study in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement.

## Data source and analytic sample

KDHS 2022 is a nationally representative household survey implemented by the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics and partners using a stratified two-stage sample design [@kdhs2022report]. This analysis used the person recode file (`PR`; `KEPR8CFL.DTA`) because it contains household-member insurance information for eligible household members in the full household questionnaire. In KDHS 2022, the insurance and disability modules were collected in the full household questionnaire, which covered about half of de-facto household members. Of `r format(analysis_object$defacto_pr_n, big.mark = ",")` de-facto household members listed in the PR file (`hv103 = 1`), `r format(analysis_object$overall_n, big.mark = ",")` had valid responses to the insurance coverage item (`sh27`) and constituted the analytic sample.

## Measures

The primary outcome was any current health insurance coverage (`sh27`). Secondary descriptive outcomes were NHIF coverage among insured members (`sh28a`), hospital admission in the past 12 months (`sh29`), outpatient use in the past 4 weeks (`sh31`), and whether money was paid at the last outpatient visit (`sh32`). We interpret `sh32` as payment at the last outpatient contact rather than a direct measure of catastrophic expenditure.

Age was grouped into eight life-course categories: under 5, 5-14, 15-17, 18-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-59, and 60 years or older. These bands were chosen for policy relevance to child, young-adult transition, and older-adult monitoring before and during SHA implementation rather than to reproduce administrative eligibility rules exactly. Wealth quintile (`hv270`), residence (`hv025`), education (`hv106`, adults aged 15 years and above), region (collapsed from county codes to the eight former provinces), sex (`hv104`), and household relationship (`hv101`) were treated as covariates.

Functional-difficulty status was derived from `hdis9`, a household-module summary variable that reflects the highest reported level of difficulty across the Washington Group Short Set domains [@washington2016]. We classified it as no difficulty, some difficulty, and a lot of difficulty or cannot do. For regression, we used a binary indicator for any difficulty versus none. Because `hdis9` was not collected for under-five children and was only available in the full household questionnaire, disability-specific analyses are not fully population-wide in the same way as the insurance estimates.

To assess the depth of financial protection rather than only whether any payment occurred, we used the continuous cost items in the household questionnaire: total outpatient cost at the last visit (`sh304`) and total inpatient cost at the last overnight admission (`sh204`), together with the amounts met by cash, NHIF, private insurance, in-kind, and other means (`sh305a`–`sh305e` for outpatient and `sh205a`–`sh205e` for inpatient). DHS reserved codes for "don't know" and "missing" occupy the highest values of each field and must be removed before any cost calculation, because they otherwise dominate the mean; for example, the uncleaned mean of `sh304` exceeds 500,000 KES against a median of 500 KES. We set reserved codes to missing at the correct field width for each variable: 9999998 and 9999999 for the seven-digit total-cost items and 999998 and 999999 for the six-digit component items. From the cleaned values we derived the cash share of total cost (cash amount divided by total cost) and the NHIF share (NHIF-met amount divided by total cost) among users with a positive recorded cost.

Household receipt of social assistance was captured from items recording assistance from the national government (`sh134aa`), county government (`sh134ab`), non-governmental or community-based organisations (`sh134ac`), and religious organisations (`sh134ad`). We defined a government cash-transfer indicator (national or county assistance) and an any-organised-safety-net indicator (government, NGO/CBO, or religious assistance, excluding informal kin support), because government transfer registries are the administrative channel that SHA premium subsidies for indigent and vulnerable persons are intended to build on.

## Statistical analysis

All estimates used household sample weights, primary sampling units, and strata from the PR file. We first estimated survey-weighted prevalence of insurance coverage, insurance type, service use, and payment at outpatient contact overall and across key subgroups. We then fitted two survey-weighted quasi-Poisson generalized linear models with log links to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (APR) for any insurance coverage [@zou2004]. Because insurance coverage is a common outcome, odds ratios from logistic regression would overstate prevalence ratios, so we estimated prevalence ratios directly with a log link. We used the quasi-Poisson rather than the log-binomial family because the survey-weighted quasi-Poisson model already provides design-robust (sandwich) variance estimates appropriate for a binary outcome [@zou2004]. In our data the fully adjusted log-binomial model did not converge—with a common outcome and very strong wealth associations, the log link produced fitted probabilities above one—which is the standard rationale for the modified-Poisson approach. To provide a convergent cross-check, we compared the two model families on a parsimonious specification (wealth and residence) in which the log-binomial converged, and the prevalence ratios agreed closely (Additional file 2, Table S6). Model A included all ages and adjusted for age group, sex, wealth quintile, residence, and region, using ages 25-34 as the reference age group. Model B was restricted to respondents aged 15 years and above and additionally adjusted for education and functional-difficulty status. Observations with missing values on model covariates were excluded under a complete-case approach; Model A included `r format(analysis_object$model_A_n, big.mark = ",")` members and Model B included `r format(analysis_object$model_B_n, big.mark = ",")` members. To test whether households already linked to social assistance were more likely to be insured, we added the government cash-transfer indicator to the all-ages specification.

Wealth-related inequality in insurance coverage was quantified using concentration indices ordered by household wealth quintile rank [@wagstaff1991; @erreygers2009; @wagstaff2011binary]. Because insurance is a bounded binary outcome, we report the standard concentration index as the main descriptive measure and the Erreygers-corrected index as a sensitivity estimate. We also estimated the slope index of inequality (SII) and relative index of inequality (RII) using weighted wealth ridit scores to summarize absolute and relative coverage differences across the full wealth distribution [@who2013handbook]. Confidence intervals for the concentration indices were derived from 250 bootstrap replicates.

To identify the drivers of wealth-related inequality, we performed a Wagstaff decomposition of the standard concentration index [@wagstaff2003decomposition]. The concentration index is expressed as the sum across determinants of the elasticity-weighted concentration index of each determinant, $C = \sum_k (\beta_k \bar{x}_k / \mu) C_k + GC_\varepsilon / \mu$, where $\beta_k$ is the coefficient of determinant $x_k$ in a survey-weighted linear probability model for coverage, $\bar{x}_k$ its mean, $\mu$ the mean of coverage, $C_k$ the concentration index of the determinant ordered by wealth rank, and $GC_\varepsilon$ the generalized concentration index of the residual. This partitions the overall inequality into the contributions of wealth, age, sex, residence, and region, with a supplementary decomposition among adults adding education and functional difficulty.

For temporal context, we compared the 2022 baseline with KDHS 2014. A like-for-like all-population (person-recode) comparison is not possible because KDHS 2014 did not carry a household-roster insurance item and the 2022 individual recodes no longer carry the individual insurance item. We therefore compared the two populations measured in both rounds—women aged 15–49 and men aged 15–54—using the 2014 individual self-reported insurance items (`v481`, `mv481`) against the same age–sex groups in the 2022 person recode. These comparisons are directional rather than exact because the respondent unit, sample weights, and wealth-index construction differ across rounds.

We also calculated the weighted composition of the uninsured population across overlapping policy-priority groups; these shares are descriptive and should not be summed across groups.

We extended the baseline with three further analyses. First, to test whether exclusion was concentrated at the intersection of social positions rather than along single axes, we conducted an intersectional multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy (MAIHDA) [@evans2018; @merlo2018]. Individuals were nested within strata defined by the combination of age group, wealth quintile, residence, and sex (`r analysis_object$maihda_n_strata` strata), and we fitted a two-level logistic model with a random intercept for stratum. From the null (intercept-only) model we computed the variance partition coefficient (VPC) using the latent-variable method—the share of total variation attributable to differences between intersectional strata—and from a model additionally adjusting for the additive main effects of the four axes we computed the proportional change in variance (PCV). The residual share, 100 minus the PCV, approximates the contribution of intersectional interaction effects beyond the additive main effects. MAIHDA models were fitted unweighted, consistent with convention; the design-based survey-weighted prevalence ratios above are the primary effect estimates.

Second, to quantify how much of the residual variation in coverage operated at the community level and to verify that the wealth and residence gradients were robust to clustering, we fitted a multilevel mixed-effects model nesting individuals within survey clusters (`hv001`) on the all-ages Model A sample [@merlo2006]. To preserve the prevalence-ratio framing used throughout, we specified a Poisson mixed model with a log link—a multilevel extension of the modified-Poisson approach—with a random intercept for cluster, and pre-specified a logistic mixed model (odds ratios) as a fallback if it failed to converge. We report the cluster-level random-intercept variance and a variance partition coefficient (a Poisson-lognormal VPC evaluated at the reference covariate pattern for the Poisson model, or the latent-variable VPC for the logistic fallback) alongside the multilevel and single-level effect estimates.

Third, to translate the equity baseline into a forward-looking policy question, we conducted a microsimulation of SHA premium-subsidy scenarios. Holding the observed wealth ranking fixed, we recomputed the standard concentration index of coverage under three counterfactual enrolment scenarios: full (100%) enrolment of everyone in the two poorest wealth quintiles; partial (80%) enrolment of those currently uninsured in the two poorest quintiles; and enrolment of all members of households already receiving a government cash transfer (the registries on which SHA premium subsidies build). Comparing each simulated index with the observed baseline indicates whether subsidising the poorest would flatten the wealth gradient or whether an uninsured "missing middle" in the middle and richer quintiles would sustain it.

All analyses were conducted in R, using the `survey`, `lme4`, and `tidyverse` packages.

## Geospatial analysis

We geolocated all 1,691 survey clusters using the KDHS 2022 GPS dataset and modelled the cluster-level probability of being uninsured as a smooth function of location, using penalised-likelihood binomial generalised additive models fitted by restricted maximum likelihood in `mgcv` [@wood2017gam]. Three nested models separate raw geography from population composition: a spatial smooth alone, the smooth plus urban/rural residence, and the smooth plus urban/rural residence and cluster wealth composition. Coordinates were projected to a Lambert azimuthal equal-area system centred on Kenya so that distances behave consistently across the country, and the spatial term was a Duchon spline with a generous basis dimension whose effective complexity was selected by the smoothing penalty rather than fixed in advance.

We chose penalised additive models over Bayesian geostatistical approximations or kriging for a substantive reason rather than a computational one. The DHS programme displaces cluster coordinates before release to protect respondent confidentiality, by up to 2 km for urban clusters and up to 5 km for rural clusters, with 1% of rural clusters displaced up to 10 km [@burgert2013geographic]. Spatial structure finer than that displacement has been removed from the data by design, so a method whose appeal rests on very high resolution would be modelling noise. We therefore predicted onto a 5 km grid as a rendering choice but interpret the surface at approximately 10 km and coarser, and report substantive findings at county and sub-regional scale.

Predictions were masked to grid cells within 50 km of a sampled cluster, so that the model is never asked to extrapolate into parts of the country the survey did not visit. Hotspots of exclusion are defined as the probability that local exclusion exceeds 90%, computed from the predicted linear predictor and its standard error, rather than by thresholding the point estimate. Thresholding point estimates would preferentially flag the most sparsely sampled areas, where estimates are least certain, which inverts the intended meaning of a hotspot. We additionally computed design-based direct estimates of exclusion for all 47 counties, since `hv024` carries county in KDHS 2022, and compared them against the model-based surface. Calibration was assessed at cluster locations against observed counts and across deciles of predicted risk.

# Results

## Sample and national baseline

The analytic sample included `r analysis_object$overall_n` de-facto household members with valid insurance data. Weighted any-insurance coverage was `r fmt_pct_string(get_t1("All household members", "Any insurance % (95% CI)"))`, while `r fmt_pct_string(get_t1("All household members", "Uninsured % (95% CI)"))` remained uninsured. Among insured household members, NHIF was the dominant form of coverage at `r fmt_pct_string(get_t1("All household members", "NHIF % of insured (95% CI)"))`, whereas community-based cover was minimal. Outpatient use in the previous 4 weeks was `r fmt_pct_string(get_t1("All household members", "Outpatient use % (95% CI)"))`, and `r fmt_pct_string(get_t1("All household members", "Paid for OPD % (95% CI)"))` of outpatient users reported paying at their last outpatient visit. Women had similar coverage to men but higher recent outpatient use and higher hospital admission.

## Life-course coverage patterns

Coverage followed a marked life-course pattern rather than a simple age gradient (Table 2, Figure 1). Young adults aged 18-24 had the lowest coverage of any age group at `r fmt_pct_string(get_t2("18-24", "All: insured % (95% CI)"))`. Coverage in all three child age bands was also low: `r fmt_pct_string(get_t2("Under 5", "All: insured % (95% CI)"))` among children under 5, `r fmt_pct_string(get_t2("5-14", "All: insured % (95% CI)"))` among ages 5-14, and `r fmt_pct_string(get_t2("15-17", "All: insured % (95% CI)"))` among ages 15-17. Coverage rose sharply in the core working-age groups, peaking at `r fmt_pct_string(get_t2("45-59", "All: insured % (95% CI)"))` among ages 45-59 before falling to `r fmt_pct_string(get_t2("60+", "All: insured % (95% CI)"))` among adults aged 60 years and above. Sex differences were modest within most age bands. The heaviest recent outpatient use was observed among adults aged 60 years and above (`r fmt_pct_string(get_t2("60+", "Outpatient % (95% CI)"))`) and among children under 5 (`r fmt_pct_string(get_t2("Under 5", "Outpatient % (95% CI)"))`).

## Socioeconomic gradient in coverage

The wealth gradient was extreme (Additional file 2, Table S1; Figure 2). Coverage ranged from `r fmt_pct_string(get_t3("Wealth quintile", "Poorest"))` in the poorest quintile to `r fmt_pct_string(get_t3("Wealth quintile", "Richest"))` in the richest, an `r wealth_ratio`-fold difference. Coverage also increased strongly with education among adults aged 15 years and above, from `r fmt_pct_string(get_t3("Education (adults 15+)", "No Education"))` among people with no education to `r fmt_pct_string(get_t3("Education (adults 15+)", "Higher"))` among those with higher education. Urban residents had much higher coverage than rural residents (`r fmt_pct_string(get_t3("Residence", "Urban"))` versus `r fmt_pct_string(get_t3("Residence", "Rural"))`). Regionally, the lowest coverage was in North Eastern (`r fmt_pct_string(get_t3("Region", "North Eastern"))`) and the highest was in Nairobi (`r fmt_pct_string(get_t3("Region", "Nairobi"))`).

Detailed socioeconomic estimates are provided in Additional file 2, Table S1.

## Policy-priority groups, insurance composition, and payment exposure

Important policy-priority groups remained poorly covered (Additional file 2, Table S2). Coverage among children under 18 was `r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Children under 18"))`, and among older adults aged 60 years and above it was `r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Older adults 60+"))`. Children under 5 had the highest outpatient use within the child bands (`r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Infants/toddlers under 5", "Outpatient % (95% CI)"))`), while older adults aged 60 years and above had the highest outpatient use overall (`r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Older adults 60+", "Outpatient % (95% CI)"))`). Payment at the last outpatient visit remained high in both groups: `r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Children under 18", "Paid for OPD % (95% CI)"))` among children and `r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Older adults 60+", "Paid for OPD % (95% CI)"))` among older adults.

Functional-difficulty results showed a mismatch between need and coverage. Any functional difficulty was associated with insurance coverage of `r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Any functional difficulty"))`, which was similar to the estimate among people with no functional difficulty (`r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("No functional difficulty"))`). However, outpatient use was much higher among those with any difficulty (`r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Any functional difficulty", "Outpatient % (95% CI)"))`) and especially among those reporting a lot of difficulty or inability (`r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("A lot of difficulty / cannot do", "Outpatient % (95% CI)"))`). Payment at the last outpatient visit remained high in these groups, reaching `r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("A lot of difficulty / cannot do", "Paid for OPD % (95% CI)"))` among the most severe difficulty group.

The poorest households remained the least protected. Coverage in the two poorest wealth quintiles combined was only `r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Two poorest wealth quintiles"))`, and grandchildren living in the household had particularly low coverage at `r fmt_pct_string(get_t4("Grandchildren in household"))`. Figure 4 shows that NHIF dominated insurance composition across all age groups. Figure 5 shows that payment at the last outpatient visit remained high for both insured and uninsured users across the wealth distribution; among insured outpatient users in the richest quintile, `r richest_insured_paid` still reported paying at their last visit.

The composition analysis adds a targeting perspective (Additional file 2, Table S5; Figure 6). Children under 18 accounted for `r get_t8("Children under 18", "Share of all uninsured %")`% of all uninsured household members, while rural residents accounted for `r get_t8("Rural residents", "Share of all uninsured %")`%. `r top_uninsured_sentence` the most over-represented among the uninsured relative to its population share.

Full policy-priority group estimates are provided in Additional file 2, Table S2.

## Adjusted correlates and wealth-related inequality

In adjusted analyses, wealth remained the dominant correlate of insurance coverage (Table 3). In Model A, the richest quintile had an APR of `r get_t5("Model A: All ages", "Wealth: Richest")` relative to the poorest quintile, while even the poorer quintile had more than double the coverage of the poorest (`r get_t5("Model A: All ages", "Wealth: Poorer")`). Young adults aged 18-24 had the lowest adjusted coverage relative to adults aged 25-34 (APR `r get_t5("Model A: All ages", "Age: 18-24")`, `r fmt_p_inline("Model A: All ages", "Age: 18-24")`). Coverage was also significantly lower among children under 5 (`r get_t5("Model A: All ages", "Age: Under 5")`) and those aged 15-17 (`r get_t5("Model A: All ages", "Age: 15-17")`). Rural residents had lower descriptive coverage but higher adjusted coverage than urban residents (APR `r get_t5("Model A: All ages", "Residence: Rural")`), indicating strong compositional confounding by wealth and other covariates.

In Model B, education explained part of the wealth gradient but did not remove it. Higher education remained strongly associated with insurance coverage (`r get_t5("Model B: Adults 15+", "Education: Higher")` for higher versus no education), and the richest-versus-poorest APR remained large at `r get_t5("Model B: Adults 15+", "Wealth: Richest")`. Functional difficulty showed no strong adjusted association with coverage (APR `r get_t5("Model B: Adults 15+", "Disability: Any difficulty")`, `r fmt_p_inline("Model B: Adults 15+", "Disability: Any difficulty")`), reinforcing that the disability result is one of high need without higher coverage rather than a straightforward disability-coverage gradient.

Wealth-related inequality was pronounced under both concentration-index formulations (Additional file 2, Table S3). The overall standard concentration index was `r fmt_ci_inline("All household members", "standard")`, and the Erreygers-corrected sensitivity estimate was `r fmt_ci_inline("All household members", "erreygers")`. Inequality was greatest among children under 18 under the standard formulation (`r fmt_ci_inline("Under 18", "standard")`). Rural coverage was also highly concentrated among better-off households (`r fmt_ci_inline("Rural", "standard")`), exceeding the urban standard concentration index of `r fmt_ci_inline("Urban", "standard")`.

Absolute and relative inequality metrics told the same story (Additional file 2, Table S4). Across the full population, the SII was `r get_t7("All household members", "SII, pp (95% CI)")` percentage points and the RII was `r get_t7("All household members", "RII (95% CI)")`, indicating a large modelled coverage advantage at the top of the wealth distribution. Among children under 18, the richest-to-poorest coverage ratio was `r sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(get_t7("Children under 18", "Richest/poorest ratio")))`.

Table 3. Survey-weighted multivariable adjusted prevalence ratios for any health insurance coverage, KDHS 2022.

## Depth of out-of-pocket payment

The binary payment indicator understated how little financial protection insurance provided (Table 4). Among all recent outpatient users, the median cash payment at the last visit was `r cost_val("opd_overall_cost", "Median cash OOP, KES")` KES, cash met `r cost_val("opd_overall_cost", "Cash share of cost, %")`% of total outpatient cost, and NHIF met only `r cost_val("opd_overall_cost", "NHIF share of cost, %")`%. The cash burden was only modestly smaller among the insured (cash share `r cost_val("opd_insured_cost", "Cash share of cost, %")`%, NHIF share `r cost_val("opd_insured_cost", "NHIF share of cost, %")`%) than among the uninsured (cash share `r cost_val("opd_uninsured_cost", "Cash share of cost, %")`%), showing that NHIF financed only a small fraction of routine outpatient spending even for its own members. Inpatient costs were far larger, with a median total cost of `r cost_val("hosp_overall_cost", "Median total cost, KES")` KES; NHIF covered a larger but still incomplete share among the insured (`r cost_val("hosp_insured_cost", "NHIF share of cost, %")`% of inpatient cost), consistent with NHIF's historical orientation toward inpatient cover. The cash share of outpatient cost stayed high across the wealth distribution for both insured and uninsured users (Figure 7).

## Linkage with social safety nets

Households already receiving social assistance were not systematically linked to insurance (Table 5). Among households receiving a government cash transfer, any-insurance coverage was `r fmt_pct_string(get_t10("All household members", "Government cash transfer: yes"))`, compared with `r fmt_pct_string(get_t10("All household members", "Government cash transfer: no"))` among households without such transfers. The pattern persisted in the two poorest quintiles, where coverage among government-transfer beneficiaries was `r fmt_pct_string(get_t10("Two poorest quintiles", "Government cash transfer: yes"))` versus `r fmt_pct_string(get_t10("Two poorest quintiles", "Government cash transfer: no"))` among non-beneficiaries. After adjustment for age, sex, wealth, residence, and region, receiving a government cash transfer had an adjusted prevalence ratio of `r analysis_object$sn_apr` for insurance coverage. The weak linkage indicates that the pre-SHA architecture did not reliably convert social-assistance enrolment into health insurance, supporting the case for a unified registry that links SHA premium subsidies to existing safety-net databases.

Table 5. Health insurance coverage among households receiving social assistance, overall and in the two poorest wealth quintiles, KDHS 2022.

## Drivers of wealth-related inequality

The Wagstaff decomposition identified which determinants generated the pro-rich concentration of coverage (Table 6). The wealth quintile itself was by far the dominant contributor, accounting for `r decomp_wealth_pct`% of the total concentration index—it more than fully explained the inequality, confirming that affordability and underlying socioeconomic position, rather than spatial or demographic composition, were the binding constraint. Residence made a negative contribution (`r decomp_residence_pct`%), reflecting that once wealth is held constant rural residence is associated with higher, not lower, coverage; this partially offsets the wealth contribution. Region, age, and sex contributed little, and the unexplained residual was negligible (`r decomp_residual_pct`%). The implication is that geographic targeting alone would not close the equity gap without directly addressing affordability. A supplementary decomposition among adults additionally attributed part of the inequality to education (Additional file 2, Table S7).

Table 6. Wagstaff decomposition of the wealth-related concentration index in any health insurance coverage, KDHS 2022.

```{r}

    sprintf("Source: Kenya DHS 2022. Decomposition of the standard concentration index (%.4f).", analysis_object$decomp_ci_total),
    "Contributions are elasticity-weighted concentration indices of each determinant; positive values push coverage toward wealthier households.",
    "Determinant contributions sum to the total concentration index together with the unexplained residual."
  )
)
```

## Change since 2014

Comparison with KDHS 2014 placed the baseline in temporal context for the populations measured in both rounds (Table 7). Among women aged 15–49, coverage moved from `r fmt_pct_string(get_t12("Women 15-49", "2014 (IR)"))` in 2014 to `r fmt_pct_string(get_t12("Women 15-49", "2022 (PR)"))` in 2022, and among men aged 15–54 from `r fmt_pct_string(get_t12("Men 15-54", "2014 (MR)"))` to `r fmt_pct_string(get_t12("Men 15-54", "2022 (PR)"))`. The wealth-related concentration index remained strongly pro-rich in both rounds (women: `r get_t12("Women 15-49", "2014 (IR)", "Concentration index")` in 2014 versus `r get_t12("Women 15-49", "2022 (PR)", "Concentration index")` in 2022). These comparisons are directional only, because the 2014 figures come from individual self-report while the 2022 figures come from the household roster, and the sample weights and wealth-index construction differ across rounds.

Table 7. Health insurance coverage and wealth-related inequality among adults of reproductive/working age, KDHS 2014 versus KDHS 2022.

publication_flextable(
  table12,
  footer_lines = c(
    "Source: Kenya DHS 2014 and 2022. Survey-weighted estimates; n values are unweighted.",
    "2014 estimates use the individual self-reported insurance item (women's recode v481; men's recode mv481); 2022 estimates use the household-roster item (sh27) restricted to the same age-sex groups.",
    "Estimates are directional: respondent type, sample weights, and wealth-index construction differ across rounds.",
    "A true all-population trend is not possible because KDHS 2014 did not carry a household-roster insurance item."
  )
)
```

## Intersectional inequality across social positions

Insurance exclusion was strongly patterned by the intersection of social positions (Table 8, Figure 8). Across the `r analysis_object$maihda_n_strata` strata defined by age group, wealth quintile, residence, and sex, the null-model variance partition coefficient was `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * analysis_object$maihda_vpc_null)`%, indicating that roughly a third of the total variation in individual coverage lay between intersectional strata rather than within them. Adjusting for the additive main effects of the four axes reduced the between-stratum variance by `r sprintf("%.1f", analysis_object$maihda_pcv)`% (the proportional change in variance), leaving only about `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 - analysis_object$maihda_pcv)`% attributable to intersectional interaction effects. The steep inequalities were therefore overwhelmingly additive—driven above all by wealth—rather than arising from specific multiplicative combinations of identities. The caterpillar plot (Figure 8) shows the resulting fan of predicted coverage across strata, with the lowest-coverage strata concentrated among poorer, rural, and younger groups.

Table 8. Intersectional multilevel analysis (MAIHDA) of any health insurance coverage across strata of age, wealth, residence, and sex, KDHS 2022.

    "VPC = variance partition coefficient (latent-variable method); PCV = proportional change in the between-stratum variance after adjusting for the additive main effects of age, wealth, residence, and sex.",
    "The residual share (100 - PCV) approximates the contribution of intersectional interaction effects beyond additive main effects."
  )
)
```

## Community-level clustering and multilevel estimates

The wealth and residence gradients were robust to community-level clustering (Table 9). A multilevel mixed model nesting individuals within survey clusters (`r analysis_object$mlm_family` specification) yielded estimates close to the design-based single-level prevalence ratios—for example, a richest-versus-poorest estimate of `r get_t15("Wealth: Richest vs Poorest")` against the single-level `r get_t15("Wealth: Richest vs Poorest", "Single-level APR (95% CI)")`, and a rural-versus-urban estimate of `r get_t15("Residence: Rural vs Urban")` against `r get_t15("Residence: Rural vs Urban", "Single-level APR (95% CI)")`. The cluster-level random-intercept variance was `r sprintf("%.3f", analysis_object$mlm_cluster_var)`, corresponding to a variance partition coefficient of `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * analysis_object$mlm_vpc)`%. Only a small share of the residual variation in coverage therefore operated between clusters once individual wealth, age, sex, residence, and region were accounted for, reinforcing that the gradient is driven by household socioeconomic position rather than by unobserved community-level factors.

Table 9. Multilevel (individuals within survey clusters) versus single-level adjusted effect estimates for any health insurance coverage, KDHS 2022.

## Microsimulation of SHA subsidy scenarios

A microsimulation of premium-subsidy scenarios showed that subsidising the poorest alone would over-correct rather than equalise the distribution of coverage (Table 10, Figure 9). At baseline the standard concentration index was strongly pro-rich (`r sprintf("%.4f", analysis_object$sim_baseline_ci)`). Enrolling 100% of the two poorest quintiles raised simulated coverage to `r get_t16("100% of poorest two quintiles enrolled", "Simulated coverage %")`% and flipped the index to pro-poor (`r get_t16("100% of poorest two quintiles enrolled", "Standard CI (95% CI)")`), because the middle and richer quintiles—still only partly insured—would then sit below the subsidised poor. An 80% enrolment scenario produced a similar reversal (coverage `r get_t16("80% of poorest two quintiles enrolled", "Simulated coverage %")`%; index `r get_t16("80% of poorest two quintiles enrolled", "Standard CI (95% CI)")`). Targeting only households already receiving a government cash transfer raised coverage modestly to `r get_t16("Government safety-net beneficiaries enrolled", "Simulated coverage %")`% and left the distribution pro-rich (`r get_t16("Government safety-net beneficiaries enrolled", "Standard CI (95% CI)")`), reflecting the limited reach of existing transfer registries. Taken together, the scenarios show that an income-neutral distribution requires reaching the uninsured "missing middle" in the middle and richer quintiles in addition to subsidising the poorest (Figure 9).

Table 10. Microsimulation of SHA premium-subsidy scenarios: coverage and the wealth-related concentration index under counterfactual enrolment, KDHS 2022.

    "A concentration index near zero indicates an income-neutral distribution; a persisting positive index reflects an uninsured 'missing middle' in the middle and richer quintiles."

)

## The geography of exclusion

All 1,691 clusters carried valid GPS coordinates. Location alone explained 50.3% of the deviance in cluster-level insurance exclusion; adding urban/rural residence raised this to 55.3%, and adding cluster wealth composition to 68.1%. The spatial smooth nevertheless remained strongly significant in the fully adjusted model (effective degrees of freedom 207.4, chi-squared 3116, p < 0.001), so where a person lives predicts exclusion well beyond what settlement type and household wealth account for. Urban clusters had substantially lower odds of exclusion than rural clusters (log-odds -0.79, standard error 0.03).

The model was well calibrated. The population-weighted national estimate implied at cluster locations was 74.1%, against 73.9% observed, and the largest discrepancy across deciles of predicted risk was 2.2 percentage points.

The predicted surface (Figure 8a) concentrates exclusion in the arid and semi-arid north and north-east and along much of the coast, with the lowest exclusion in Nairobi and the central highlands. Of the sampled domain, which covers 22,136 of 23,634 5 km land cells or 93.7% of Kenya, 55.6% had at least an 80% probability that local exclusion exceeded 90% (Figure 8b). The residual surface net of settlement type and wealth composition (Figure 8d) retains the same north-east to central gradient, indicating that the geography of exclusion is not simply a map of where poor or rural households happen to live.

County-level direct estimates (Table 17, Figure 8e) span a far wider range than the eight former provinces reported above: from 94.7% (95% CI 92.4% to 97.0%) uninsured in Tana River, 94.0% (91.1% to 96.9%) in Mandera and 93.1% (89.9% to 96.3%) in Marsabit, to 54.0% (47.8% to 60.2%) in Nairobi, 57.3% (51.4% to 63.2%) in Nyeri and 57.8% (52.2% to 63.5%) in Kiambu, a spread of 40.7 percentage points. All 47 counties had direct 95% confidence intervals narrower than 20 percentage points, so county-level reporting is supportable from this survey without model-based smoothing.

# Discussion

This study provides a population-wide pre-SHA baseline for insurance coverage and wealth-related inequality in Kenya. Three findings stand out. First, overall insurance coverage remained low at `r fmt_pct_string(get_t1("All household members", "Any insurance % (95% CI)"))`, with almost three quarters of the population uninsured. Second, coverage was extremely pro-rich by both regression and concentration-index evidence. Third, payment at the last outpatient visit remained high even among insured users, indicating that insurance enrolment alone did not eliminate point-of-care payment.

The life-course pattern is especially important for policy. Young adults aged 18-24 had the lowest coverage of any age group, lower than children and lower than older adults. That pattern is plausible in light of broader evidence that young people in low- and middle-income countries face access barriers during transitions from schooling to work and from parental dependency to independent household formation [@nachiappan2022]. In the Kenyan context, the Act and General Regulations create multiple routes to coverage, including contributor registration, dependant coverage, and government-financed coverage for indigent and vulnerable persons, but these routes still depend on administrative identification and household or individual registration processes [@socialhealthinsuranceact2023; @shigeneralregulations2024]. The survey age bands in this paper therefore identify groups that matter for monitoring, but they should not be read as direct administrative entitlement counts.

Wealth-related exclusion remained the defining structural feature of coverage. The descriptive richest-to-poorest ratio of `r wealth_ratio`x, all-ages APR of `r get_t5("Model A: All ages", "Wealth: Richest")`, SII of `r get_t7("All household members", "SII, pp (95% CI)")` percentage points, and RII of `r get_t7("All household members", "RII (95% CI)")` indicate that Kenya entered the SHA era with a sharply stratified pre-existing enrolment base. This is consistent with prior Kenyan and sub-Saharan African evidence showing that insurance expansion under contributory or mixed systems tends to favor better-off households [@kimani2014; @kazungu2017; @barasa2021]. The finding that rural residence became positively associated with coverage after adjustment does not contradict the lower descriptive rural coverage. Instead, it implies that rural disadvantage is largely compositional, driven by the concentration of poorer households in rural areas. The very high rural concentration index and the uninsured-composition analysis support that interpretation.

The inequality estimates also help place Kenya in a regional monitoring frame. Barasa and colleagues showed that insurance coverage across sub-Saharan Africa was typically low and pro-rich, with wealth-related concentration reflecting the difficulty of expanding contributory insurance to poorer and informal-sector households [@barasa2021]. Our pre-SHA concentration index of `r fmt_ci_inline("All household members", "standard")` is consistent with that pattern, while the SII of `r get_t7("All household members", "SII, pp (95% CI)")` percentage points translates the same inequality into an absolute coverage gap that is easier for policy audiences to interpret.

The disability findings sharpen the distinction between coverage and need. People with any functional difficulty had similar coverage to people with no difficulty, and the adjusted association between functional difficulty and insurance was weak. Yet their outpatient use was much higher, and point-of-care payment remained high, particularly for those reporting a lot of difficulty or inability. This pattern is consistent with recent systematic review evidence showing that disability-related need in low- and middle-income countries is not reliably matched by insurance inclusion or financial protection [@azizatunnisa2024]. For SHA, the operational implication is not simply to cover disability in principle, but to build workable registration and verification systems that identify high-need persons without creating new access barriers.

The high payment rate at outpatient contact is also important. In this study, `r fmt_pct_string(get_t1("All household members", "Paid for OPD % (95% CI)"))` of recent outpatient users reported paying at their last visit, and payment remained common across wealth groups and across insurance status. Examining the depth rather than only the occurrence of payment sharpened this conclusion: cash met roughly `r cost_val("opd_overall_cost", "Cash share of cost, %")`% of total outpatient cost and NHIF only about `r cost_val("opd_overall_cost", "NHIF share of cost, %")`%, and the cash share among insured outpatient users was nearly as high as among the uninsured. In other words, even where NHIF membership existed, it financed little of the routine outpatient bill, and protection was concentrated in inpatient care. This measure is not equivalent to catastrophic spending, but it does indicate that routine outpatient care still involved substantial direct payment for most users. That result is aligned with broader evidence that insurance growth in low- and middle-income countries does not necessarily translate into strong financial protection and with Kenyan analyses showing persistent gaps between enrolment, benefit design, provider payment, and effective access [@hooley2022; @mbau2020; @barasa2018]. It is also consistent with implementation evidence from Kenya's UHC pilot, which documented persistent challenges around benefit-package clarity, funding flows, provider autonomy, and commodity availability even where user-fee reforms were being pursued [@nyawira2024]. For SHA, the Primary Healthcare Fund's promise of free primary care will only translate into financial protection if it displaces these cash payments at the outpatient point of care rather than sitting alongside them.

The decomposition and safety-net findings point to concrete policy levers. The wealth quintile more than fully explained the pro-rich concentration of coverage, while region contributed little and residence acted in the opposite direction once wealth was held constant. This means the binding constraint before SHA was affordability rather than geography; subsidy design, not only facility distribution, is therefore central to closing the gap. Yet households already receiving government cash transfers—the very group SHA premium subsidies are meant to reach—were only weakly more likely to be insured, even among the poorest two quintiles. This signals a coordination failure between social-assistance registries and the pre-SHA insurance system. SHA's reliance on means-testing and existing vulnerability databases to finance indigent coverage will succeed only if that linkage is built deliberately, so that enrolment in a cash-transfer programme automatically triggers health-insurance registration.

The comparison with KDHS 2014 indicates that, for women aged 15–49 and men aged 15–54, the wealth-related concentration of coverage remained strongly pro-rich across nearly a decade of NHIF reform. Although the 2014 and 2022 figures are not strictly comparable because of differences in respondent unit and survey instruments, the persistence of a steep gradient suggests that incremental contributory expansion did not, on its own, dismantle the structural inequality that SHA now inherits.

For SHA monitoring, the practical implication is that enrolment totals should be paired with distributional indicators. The indicators in this paper can be repeated as SHA implementation data mature: coverage in the poorest quintile, coverage among children under 18, coverage among young adults aged 18-24, coverage among people with severe functional difficulty, the wealth-related SII/RII, and payment at the last outpatient contact among insured users. These indicators do not determine eligibility for government-financed SHA coverage, but they identify groups for which registration, contribution subsidy, provider payment, and benefit-package implementation should be monitored together.

The intersectional, multilevel, and microsimulation analyses converge on the same policy message from different angles. The MAIHDA results show that pre-SHA exclusion was structured overwhelmingly by the additive effect of wealth rather than by idiosyncratic combinations of identities: about a third of the variation in individual coverage lay between intersectional strata, yet adjusting for the four axes' main effects removed almost all of it, leaving a negligible interaction component [@evans2018; @merlo2018]. The multilevel model points the same way—once individual socioeconomic position was accounted for, very little residual variation operated between survey clusters, and the multilevel prevalence ratios were almost identical to the design-based estimates, so the steep wealth gradient is not an artefact of community-level clustering [@merlo2006]. The microsimulation then makes the operational implication concrete. Subsidising only the two poorest quintiles did not merely narrow the gap but reversed it, because the partially insured middle and richer quintiles were left behind; targeting existing cash-transfer registries alone reached too few people to move the distribution. For SHA, this means that financing indigent coverage is necessary but not sufficient: an income-neutral coverage distribution also requires deliberately enrolling the uninsured "missing middle" of informal-sector and lower-middle-wealth households that fall outside both formal employment and means-tested subsidy.

## Strengths and limitations

The main strengths of this study are its population-wide scope, its use of the PR file to analyze all ages and both sexes together, its focus on survey-weighted estimates across the full age distribution, and its inclusion of complementary inequality metrics: concentration indices, Erreygers-corrected estimates, SII, RII, a Wagstaff decomposition, and composition of the uninsured population. By analyzing the depth of out-of-pocket payment rather than only its occurrence, examining linkage with social safety nets, and benchmarking against KDHS 2014, the study moves beyond a single descriptive cross-section. The intersectional MAIHDA, multilevel, and subsidy microsimulation analyses further strengthen the inference by showing that the wealth gradient is additive and robust to clustering, and by translating it into actionable subsidy-targeting scenarios. The life-course framing also makes the results directly relevant to monitoring SHA implementation.

Several limitations matter. First, the study is cross-sectional and cannot support causal claims about the determinants of coverage. Second, insurance, service use, costs, and payment at the last outpatient visit were self-reported and may be subject to recall or reporting error; the cost items in particular contained reserved "don't know" codes and a minority of records in which the reported cash payment exceeded the reported total cost, which is why we summarized cost shares as population-level aggregates rather than averages of individual ratios. Third, the insurance, cost, and disability modules were collected only in the full household questionnaire, so the analytic sample represents that subsample of de-facto household members rather than the entire household roster. Selection into the full household questionnaire subsample was determined by the KDHS 2022 sampling design, and we used the household-member weights provided for that subsample, so it is not expected to introduce systematic bias within the survey's design-based inference framework; nonetheless, residual selection concerns cannot be entirely ruled out. Fourth, disability-specific analyses are additionally limited because the household disability summary variable was not collected for under-five children. Fifth, the payment and cost analyses are conditional on recent care-seeking—outpatient use in the previous 4 weeks or admission in the previous 12 months—which is itself wealth-dependent. Poorer or uninsured individuals who forgo or delay care because they cannot pay are not observed among users, so the payment-exposure estimates are conditional on having sought care and may understate the true financial barrier faced by the poorest; insured and uninsured users may also differ in underlying need. These estimates also do not capture total household spending or catastrophic expenditure. Sixth, the KDHS 2014 comparison is restricted to women aged 15–49 and men aged 15–54 and relies on a different insurance instrument and respondent unit, so it indicates direction rather than precise change. Seventh, KDHS 2022 was conducted before SHA became operational, so the analysis cannot capture early SHA registration, contribution assessment, or claims experience. Eighth, the survey groups examined here are policy-relevant monitoring categories, not exact administrative counts of who qualifies for government-financed SHA coverage under current legal and operational rules. Ninth, the multilevel and MAIHDA models were fitted unweighted, as is conventional for variance-partitioning models, so their variance components complement rather than replace the design-based weighted prevalence ratios; the Poisson-lognormal variance partition coefficient is also mean-dependent and was evaluated at the reference covariate pattern. Tenth, the subsidy microsimulation is a deterministic counterfactual that holds the observed wealth ranking and all other behaviour fixed and assumes enrolment translates directly into the coverage indicator; it is intended to illustrate the distributional logic of alternative targeting rules rather than to forecast actual SHA uptake, costs, or service use.

# Conclusions

Before SHA, Kenya had low overall insurance coverage, strong wealth-related inequality, and widespread payment at outpatient contact. The most excluded populations were not defined by one single category: young adults had the lowest coverage, children had the highest wealth-related inequality, older adults had the highest recent outpatient use, and people with severe functional difficulty had high need without a clear coverage advantage. SHA implementation should therefore be evaluated against a broad monitoring framework that includes life-course coverage, wealth gradients, disability-sensitive access, and payment at the point of outpatient care.

# List of abbreviations

- APR: adjusted prevalence ratio
- CI: concentration index or confidence interval, depending on context
- DHS: Demographic and Health Survey

- NHIF: National Hospital Insurance Fund

- PR: person recode
- SHA: Social Health Authority
- STROBE: Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology
